summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option that tells a client the longest time it should wait before asking again for configuration information. It is meant for stateless DHCPv6, where no leases exist to tell the client when to refresh. This standards-track document was later replaced by RFC 8415.

eli5.summary: A reminder note on a fridge saying check again for updates after this long. Without it, a device that gets settings once might never ask again.

questions: how often should dhcpv6 clients refresh
what is the dhcpv6 information refresh time option
how often does a dhcpv6 client refresh
subtitle: A DHCPv6 option that tells a client the longest it should wait before asking for its configuration again.

tldr.problem: With stateless DHCPv6 the configuration data has no lifetime, so nothing tells a host when to ask the server for it again.
tldr.mechanism: The server puts an information refresh time option, a 32-bit number of seconds, in its Reply to an Information-Request. The client treats it as an upper bound on how long to wait before refreshing.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can bound how long clients keep stale settings, for example during renumbering. The document was later obsoleted by RFC 8415.

today: RFC 4242 was a Proposed Standard published in November 2005 and has been obsoleted by RFC 8415, which is now the place to look for this option.

sections.title: Why a Refresh Time Is Needed
sections.content:
Many IPv6 hosts pick their address with stateless autoconfiguration and use DHCPv6 only for other settings, as described in RFC 3736. Those settings usually have no lifetime attached, so a host has no hint about when to refresh them.

The RFC lists three situations where a refresh time helps: unstable environments where changes are likely, planned changes such as renumbering (an administrator can gradually decrease the time as the event nears), and limiting how long it takes for a new service or server to become available, such as a new NTP server or a changed DNS server address.
sections.eli5: If nobody tells you when your homework list changes, you might never look again. This option says look again after this much time.

sections.title: How the Option Works
sections.content:
The information refresh time option gives an upper bound on how long a client should wait before refreshing information from DHCPv6. It is only used in Reply messages that answer Information-Request messages. In other messages there are usually other options, such as addresses with lifetimes, that say when to contact the server.

It is only an upper bound. A client may refresh sooner, for instance when an application needs more configuration parameters, when a router announces a new IPv6 prefix, or when the client suspects it moved to a new link. In that case it should refresh all of its data.

One refresh time covers all the data, because a client that has a reason to refresh some of it should refresh the rest. Expiry does not mean the client must delete its data. It keeps the current data while trying to refresh, though it may fall back to other mechanisms if it cannot refresh in a reasonable time. A new Reply replaces the old configuration, including removing information the new Reply leaves out.
sections.eli5: The timer is a maximum, like saying call me at least once a day. You can call earlier, and you keep your old notes until the new ones arrive.

sections.title: Client and Server Rules
sections.content:
Two constants are defined. IRT_DEFAULT is 86400 (24 hours) and implementations SHOULD allow it to be configured. IRT_MINIMUM is 600.

A client MUST request the option in the Option Request Option (ORO) of its Information-Request messages and MUST NOT request it in any other message. If the Reply lacks the option, the client behaves as if it had received IRT_DEFAULT. If the value is below IRT_MINIMUM, the client MUST use IRT_MINIMUM. The value 0xffffffff means infinity: no refresh without some other trigger, such as moving to a new link.

When the time expires, the client SHOULD send an Information-Request, but MUST first wait a random delay between 0 and INF_MAX_DELAY. A client MAY also set its own maximum refresh time, used whenever it receives a larger value or infinity.

A server SHOULD include the option in a Reply if the ORO requested it. The value MUST NOT be smaller than IRT_MINIMUM, the server SHOULD warn if configured with a smaller one, and the option MUST only appear in the options area of Reply messages.
sections.eli5: If no time is given, assume one day. Never check more often than every ten minutes, and wait a random moment before asking so everyone does not knock at once.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
The option has a 16-bit option-code, a 16-bit option-len and a 32-bit information-refresh-time. The code is OPTION_INFORMATION_REFRESH_TIME (32), the length is 4, and the time is a duration relative to the current time, in seconds.

IANA assigned the option code from the DHCPv6 option-code space.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny labelled card: a label saying what it is, a size, and a number of seconds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The option does not change the DHCPv6 security considerations in any significant way. An attacker could send forged Replies with a very low refresh time, but the IRT_MINIMUM floor limits that threat. An attacker could also send a very large value so the client keeps forged information for a long time. The RFC suggests that a client may enforce a maximum to reduce this problem.
sections.eli5: A trickster could say never check again, so a careful device sets its own longest wait.

fields.name: information-refresh-time
fields.desc: Duration relative to now, in seconds.
